moderators.variable: Type of Scene (Natural vs Built Environments)
moderators.effect: Significant moderation for coherence (natural r=0.31, built r=0.72) and legibility (natural r=-0.25, built r=0.52); no significant moderation for complexity and mystery.

final_result.publication_bias: Selective reporting of results (publication bias) is a concern, as journals often enforced a 'p<0.05' criterion, leading to small effects being excluded from the collective literature. This suggests that the point estimates of collective correlations presented in the results may be upper boundaries.

final_result.title: Twenty years after Hines, Hungerford, and Tomera: A new meta-analysis of psycho-social determinants of pro-environmental behaviour

moderators.variable: Type of pro-environmental behaviour / Kind of sample
moderators.effect: Statistical tests indicated strong heterogeneity (Q-statistic p < .0016 for most correlations), suggesting associations vary considerably across different types of pro-environmental behaviour or sample characteristics. Further moderator analyses are needed but limited by available data.

final_result.publication_bias: Funnel plots for intention-behaviour correlations showed a 'hole' in the low left part of the distribution, with only two out of 15 correlations below .20, suggesting a potential bias from not reporting low insignificant intention-behaviour correlations. For other correlations (attitude-intention, moral norm-intention, PBC-intention), funnel plots were consistent with the expected pattern.

final_result.title: Evidence for prospect-refuge theory: a meta-analysis of the findings of environmental preference research

moderators.effect: Support for prospect is strongest in interior settings. Refuge is least supported in interior settings (mostly neutral findings). Mystery findings are less emphatic (mostly neutral or contrary). Complexity is preferred in interior space, but the degree/location is unclear. Results are most valid in specific venues.
Landscape and urban studies were more common in the 1980s-1990s, while interior studies (especially computational/combined approaches) are more recent.

final_result.publication_bias: Small studies are widely cited, but larger studies tended to have more neutral results, raising concerns about usefulness.

moderators.effect: Significant difference in average effect size for positive affect, with largest effects observed in studies conducted in Japan (r=0.51), followed by United States (r=0.32), Canada (r=0.24), and Sweden (r=0.15).

moderators.variable: Type of natural environment (managed vs. wild)
moderators.effect: No significant moderation on positive affect.
No significant moderation on positive affect.
Significant positive association with positive affect, indicating larger effects were observed in studies using older samples.

final_result.publication_bias: For positive affect, Duval and Tweedie's trim and fill approach suggested a possible bias to overestimate the effect (adjusted r=0.30), but Egger's regression test was nonsignificant (p=0.08), indicating either a lack of bias or a slight bias by underrepresenting small effect sizes. For negative affect, trim and fill indicated no missing studies and Egger's test was nonsignificant (p=0.46), indicating a lack of bias.
